title: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack
description: Image source, ReutersByLily JamaliNorth America Technology correspondentTwo major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointin
body: Image source, ReutersByLily JamaliNorth America Technology correspondentTwo major blockchain analytics firms say they have robust intelligence pointing to a North Korean state-backed group as the likely culprits in the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) hack of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.The Lazarus Group, a North Korean hacking unit also known as TraderTraitor, was identified "with high confidence" by TRM Labs, as well as Chainalysis.This incident is just the latest linked to the country, one of the poorest in the world and where access to the internet is severely restricted.Experts accuse the government of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un of relying on cybercrime to finance itself, something Pyongyang has long denied.Though not financial, the nation's most spectacular suspected hack took place in 2014. The target: Sony Pictures, which had made the Hollywood film The Interview. The film involves a plot to assassinate Kim. The resulting hack exposed thousands of embarrassing emails exchanged among the studio's top executives.Last year, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said North Korea was responsible for the theft of $1.5bn on the Bybit exchange.In the aftermath of that incident, the agency said TraderTraitor had moved to quickly launder and disperse the stolen assets, converting them to Bitcoin and other digital assets with a goal of eventually turning them into hard currency.The FBI has broadly accused North Korea of "illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities".The nation has systematically developed its cyber operations, recruiting the most promising students from universities and channeling them into hacker groups overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, according to reports.Some of the cyberwarfare conducted takes place just over the nation's border in China, according to analysis from tech groups.Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affectedMuch of its hacking activity has centred on monetary gain.North Korean hackers are also suspected in the theft of $620m worth of cryptocurrency in 2022.In this most recent heist, North Korean agents are accused of using a special authorisation to turn a Binance hot wallet, which is connected to the internet, into one that moved funds automatically to the attacker.TRM said it's likely the attacker gained access to Binance's hot wallet signing system as part of the scheme.Binance  has not directly responded to the BBC's queries about the incident's potential links to the area.The company had initially said it thought an engineer's laptop had been compromised, allowing unauthorised withdrawals, but later said the attack was wider."Our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach," Binance's co-CEO Richard Teng said.Some 80% of stolen assets have been secured, a Binance spokesperson said on Friday, but the rest remains unaccounted for.If the accusations are true, the record-making heist shows how powerful suspected North Korean hackers have become – a sign that the tools of the hacking trade have grown sharper.Experts say the rise of artificial intelligence has also given threat actors new ways to carry out crime, through automation and other means.In this case, it's plausible that AI was used to infiltrate Binance's systems.As Chainalysis put it, the attacker used laundering patterns "we have not seen before".

schema.headline: Why North Korea's 'elite' hackers are the prime suspect in major Binance hack

title: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue
description: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social me
body: In Armenia's capital this week a fight between politicians broke out - not the mass brawl in its parliament that was so widely documented on social media - but between delegates from nearly 200 countries. The world's nations have been gathered in Yerevan for nearly two weeks  negotiating, and arguing, over a new agreement on nature.Early on Saturday morning, hours after talks were due to finish, they finally agreed the key parts of a new action plan. "And that's it. Perfect," said the meeting president, Hambardzum Matevosyan. Four years earlier the same countries had signed a landmark deal committing to "halt and reverse" the decline of nature. That global deal in 2022 - the Global Biodiversity Framework - contained 24 targets including putting 30% of the world's land and seas into protection by the end of the decade.They agreed that action was urgent. The world is currently in a sixth mass extinction event with species becoming extinct at 100 times the natural rate because of human activities, scientists say.But according to the UN this week,, external the world is on track to achieve just one of those two dozen targets. As part of this week's deal, countries acknowledged they were falling behind."While not particularly exciting or detailed, it's good news that countries could reach agreement," said Catherine Weller, from environmental charity Fauna & Flora."We cannot just plod on to 2030 without a course correction; nature is critical to all life on Earth: to our economies, to our wellbeing," she added. This was echoed by Craig Bennett, CEO of The Wildlife Trusts, who told BBC News: "We are still seeing an appalling loss, threatening the collapse of ecosystems globally. We run out of words really about how serious this is."But he added "the better news is there are so many examples worldwide about how... to turn things around".Countries have put 623 million acres (252m hectares) of degraded land into protection, external - an area bigger than Greenland. Just last month the WWF praised conservation efforts which had achieved the recovery of key species including elephants, green sea turtles and tigers.Bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWFCountries have recognised the main barrier to accelerating those efforts is money. In 2022, they agreed they would put $30bn (£22.4bn) towards nature recovery efforts by the end of the decade, and mobilise a further $170bn from private sources.But years later many nations have been redirecting international aid to defence budgets and to deal with repeated energy shocks, such that pledges are not at the rate required to reach those targets, according to the UN. , externalAt this meeting, more than $1bn was pledged, with half of that coming from philanthropists including Leonardo DiCaprio's Re:wild organisation. Anna Ducros, a researcher at the International Institute for Environment and Development, said there had been some progress on countries committing to reducing subsidies for industries harmful to the environment."A concrete example is that governments subsidise large-scale fishing that is especially harmful for nature - for example, trawling."Ducros, who was in attendance at the talks, added: "Right now, we have the situation where governments are paying twice. "So they know that they need to increase spending on nature and climate, but at the same time, they're damaging nature."A specific funding pot, the Cali Fund, was previously set up for private companies that profit from using genetic material found in the environment to donate to. It was estimated up to $3.6bn could be raised annually -  at the start of the meeting just $10,000 had been pledged.Little progress was made on that issue - its voluntary nature makes it difficult to put pressure on companies, Bennett acknowledged."When you have countries that have rich biodiversity in them and you have companies trying to make money out of the genetic material found in those countries they should be paying those communities," he said. "That should not be controversial."One of the easier issues on the agenda was meant to be the approval of scientific reports into the state of nature. But a small group of countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, were reported to have frustrated that process."The attacks on science have bothered me a lot," French Ecological Transition Minister Monique Barbut was reported as saying by the AFP news agency. Next month countries will gather for the annual climate conference - COP31. Its own science body, the IPCC, has faced similar challenges in the past month with passing its own scientific reports and securing funding."This is such a blatant political move...and the IPCC is no such place for such political manoeuvring since the outputs are in humanity's interest," said Prof David Lee, from Manchester University, who has worked on previous reports.

schema.headline: Global nature talks reach deal but money remains an issue

title: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister
description: European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, lea
body: European diplomats have refused to stand for an official photo with Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov at the G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting, leading to the American hosts cancelling the planned picture.Two officials confirmed to BBC the cancellation of the "family photo" scheduled for Friday, which usually include representatives from all nations attending."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband later told his Russian counterpart at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Speaking with G20 foreign ministers on Friday, Miliband said that member countries  must "work harder to secure just and lasting peace in Ukraine". "Russia's war continues to cause colossal global harm - including the deaths of thousands of innocent civilians and disruption that hits energy and supplies and worsens food insecurity," he said. "This war is not simply a test for Europe or for Nato - it requires all of us to apply economic and diplomatic pressure to deprive Putin of the revenues that perpetuate this barbaric war."Ukraine is not a G20 member but has been invited to similar meetings in recent years. However, Ukraine was not invited to this meeting.One British official told the BBC: "The UK has a longstanding policy not to have direct, bilateral engagement with Russian ministers since the invasion of Ukraine and we are not about to change that".Relations between Ukraine and the US have been particularly tense this month, with a diplomatic standoff between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over Kyiv's strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.A US official said the photo was cancelled "after it became clear some of the delegations were unwilling to participate in a joint photo"."Rather than allow a ceremonial photo opportunity to become a diplomatic distraction, the US decided to forgo the photo and keep the focus on the substantive discussions," the official said.In contrast to Ukraine, relations between the US and Russia appear to have partially thawed in recent weeks, as Trump waived some sanctions and agreed a deal to import Russian diesel for the American market. The move comes as Trump attempts to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of midterm elections on Tuesday, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.Ukraine and its European allies have heavily criticised Trump's deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin.Zelensky called it "a gift" to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged".Trump said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table in the war between Russia and Ukraine.Putin has said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, is willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products.Still, the US State Department this week said it had approved the sale of more than $2bn worth of Patriot missiles to Ukraine, a critically needed munition for the country's air defences to protect itself from Russian attacks.  Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory.Moscow has in recent weeks intensified its deadly missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities.

schema.headline: G20 'family photo' cancelled after protests over presence of Russian minister

title: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he is "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in the transatlantic slave trade, but has ruled out financial reparations.He said he wanted a "dialogue with those affected" and was open to "calls for an apology", but said reparations were "not the right answer".The statement was welcomed by the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) for Afrikan Reparations, with its chair Bell Ribeiro-Adday telling BBC Radio 4's Today programme the issue was not just about money.It comes ahead of next week's Commonwealth leaders summit in the Caribbean. As King Charles III tours the region, there have been renewed calls for an apology.During the first leg of his tour in the Bahamas, the King made reference to the "suffering of the past". Later, in Guyana, he visited the site of a rebellion of enslaved people against British authorities. On Saturday, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade, when Africans were trafficked to the Americas, as a "brutal and barbaric violation" and said Britain must "face up to the past".The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations. Burnham has stuck with the policy of his predecessors, and has stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments. "I do not think that British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous, that happened in a different age under different laws and in which they played no personal part," Burnham wrote in a piece for the Guardian, external.He said Commonwealth countries had for years been asking for an "honest conversation". He said he wanted to offer a "structured dialogue", adding: "Listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state will form an important part of this process. I am open to them."A government source told the BBC this was "morally the right thing to do". But APPG for Afrikan Reparations Ribeiro-Addy said while the government's acceptance of the role it played was welcomed, it had "still fallen short of a formal state apology and that actually costs nothing"."Acknowledgment is not the same as understanding," she told Today, adding: "Until we apologise, we are never going to be on equal footing… it's meant to be a family of nations - a Commonwealth - and it's simply not the case."The MP for Clapham and Brixton Hill said that, to her knowledge, an invoice for financial reparations has not been given to the UK, and so discussing "reparative justice" on those ends, was missing the point."My worry is the focus on financial reparations, and I think that is deeply problematic and has not quite listened to what people have said," Ribeiro-Addy said.Downing Street believes it is in the UK's interest to strengthen the Commonwealth, in a world where China and Russia are seeking to exert influence.Only this week, President Vladimir Putin hosted a Russia-Africa summit in Moscow. Prime Minister of Barbados Mia Mottley, who has sought reparations, welcomed Burnham's statement, saying she would engage in good faith while still seeking reparatory justice.Denis O'Brien, founder of The Repair Campaign, said Burnham's statement was disappointing and did not go far enough."The British Government must stop obfuscating and give a full and formal apology now," he said. "This would be a significant and symbolic first step towards reparatory justice." From the 16th Century, English authorities and the monarchy were prominent participants in the centuries-long slave trade.Britain had a key role in ending the trade, through Parliament's passage of a law to abolish slavery in 1833.As part of that law, British plantation owners were paid for the loss of people they had enslaved.The UK only finished paying off the debt it incurred to cover the payments in 2015.

schema.headline: Burnham 'open' to calls for slavery apology but rules out reparations

title: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
description: President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff. Nawrocki cancelled a trip t
body: President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, has now entered the constitutional court, according to his chief of staff. Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal mid-air in order to attend to the confrontation in Warsaw. He had been on his way to the Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court."All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski  to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons"."Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media. "Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

schema.headline: Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court

title: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
description: The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secu
body: The latest move comes after a row between Zelensky and Donald Trump earlier this month when the US eased sanctions on Russia as part of a deal to secure Russian diesel. The US president stated it was time for Ukraine to get a new leader to strike a deal to end the war with Russia. Moscow launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, having earlier seized Crimea and parts of Donbas in the east. Tensions eased after Zelensky held talks with US envoys in Oslo on 20 October.In Friday's statement, the State Department said "this proposed sale will support the foreign policy and national security objectives of the United States by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe".It said "Ukraine will pay for this purchase with donations from Canada, Germany, and Norway via the JUMPSTART program and national funds, financed by the European Union's Ukraine Support Loan". The statement said the "principal contractor" would be American company Lockheed Martin, adding that "no US funds are involved in this sale".Meanwhile, at the G20 foreign ministers' meeting European diplomats protested over the presence of Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov by refusing to stand for an official photograph.The meeting is being hosted in Atlanta by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio."Let me say this directly to the Russian Foreign Minister: We all know who the aggressor in this war is," UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband told Lavrov at the summit, accusing his government of killing innocent civilians in Ukraine.

schema.headline: US approves sale of 500 Patriot missiles to Ukraine

title: Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials
description: Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?Prime Ministe
body: Wander through Parliament at the moment, and there is one issue many MPs want to discuss: is there going to be an early general election?Prime Minister Andy Burnham has nearly three years to go before he has to call an election and he has repeatedly and categorically ruled out going to the country early.But the discussion persists - and many think it is a real possibility.After Wednesday's Budget, that talk has only increased.As one former Labour minister puts it: "Why would you sprinkle round a few politically smart (albeit small) giveaways now but delay all the really tough and unpopular decisions on welfare and defence to an autumn spending review if you weren't creating a window for a spring election?"Others have also suggested to the BBC that Chancellor John Healey's plans felt like a pre-election programme.They argue the Budget contained voter-friendly measures on the cost of living, such as £100 help for many with energy bills and extending VAT cuts on electricity bills. Young voters are to be offered help on to the housing ladder, through the Your First Home scheme.Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has questioned why some-voter friendly measures announced by Healey will only be in place until the summer. Could it be, she suggests, that the prime minister plans to go to the country before these measures run out? (The counter-argument to this is that household energy pressures are less severe in the summer.)Some MPs also point out the prime minister is popular at the moment and Labour is leading in most polls. Reform, who had led the polls for some time, have had a difficult few months. Will things ever look better for Burnham, they ask.There are, though, plenty of arguments against a general election in the next year.Firstly, the prime minister has repeatedly ruled it out in interviews.On Wednesday, he said explicitly that there would not be an election in the next 12 months. Politicians can change their minds, but one veteran Tory concludes a change of heart, after emphatic denials, would be too damaging to "Brand Burnham".Next – despite the chancellor's giveaways on the cost of living – the overall economic outlook is "pretty grim", in the words of the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR).Real Household Disposable Income looks set to fall in the coming months. Interest rates are predicted to go up. Nobody knows for sure what will happen next in the Middle East – and whether things could get worse before they get better.Burnham has pledged a rewiring of the British state. He plans to set out a 10-year plan in the coming weeks. But without more detail, some wonder if voters will know enough to make a judgement. On more than one occasion, Burnham has vowed to bring about the most significant change in British politics in four decades.One former Labour minister could not detect much in this week's Budget to that effect, saying: "It's not an end to 40 years of neoliberalism is it?"That message was echoed by another Labour MP: "It was too low key to be an election Budget.""It was a disappointment, a play it safe, keep everything ticking over Budget… crumbs for all," said another."No early general election after that Budget. We would be toast."Some argue Burnham would benefit from having his own mandate, with his own manifesto. But given the size of Labour's general election win last time, many MPs think it's inevitable that Labour will lose ground.Others say that if Burnham's government does feel the need to break Sir Keir Starmer's manifesto commitments by increasing taxes, they should just do it, instead of holding an election."If we need an election to put up taxes then arguably that's easier to do now with our massive majority than to start an election campaign on the basis that we're calling it in order to put up taxes," said one Labour MP."People act like a manifesto is a legal document written in blood. Plenty of governments have broken lots of manifesto promises."Remember too that the prime minister has promised a detailed plan on social care in England, which is some way off. He has also not decided how far he wants to go in taking the UK closer to the EU.There is a lot for Number 10 to weigh up.Labour might look back to Gordon Brown, who did not call an early election when he was prime minister and doing well in the polls. If he had gone to the country in October 2007, might Labour have stayed in power?But there will be plenty of others who look to Theresa May. She opted for a snap general election in April 2017, after mulling the decision over on a walking holiday in Wales. Despite flying high in the polls, the Tories lost their majority.So will Burnham do it? He might be tempted. But there are plenty of risks that mean it would be far from an easy choice.

schema.headline: Why MPs keep talking about an early election despite Burnham's denials

title: Spain train disaster clouds Pedro Sánchez chances of re-election
description: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative
body: The formal investigation into the Toledo train disaster has only just been launched but the government has been quick to take control of the narrative.From the first hours after the collision, Transport Minister Oscar Puente began suggesting "human error" was to blame, batting responsibility as far as possible from the cabinet.On Friday, he appeared before the press for a second time to set out what he called the "objective facts" of the crash and counter a surge of criticism against the government.The opposition People's Party (PP) is among those calling for his resignation as a "moral" and "ethical" move.Instead after expressing "huge pain and sadness" for the victims, Puente went on the offensive.He rejected talk of chronic underinvestment in infrastructure and insisted that Spain's high-speed signalling safety system, the LZB, was neither old nor inadequate: Germany and Austria use the same.In Spain, it has already failed 170 times so far this year, he revealed, but called that "normal" and around the EU average.The problem surrounds what happens next - when the system fails and control of the line shifts to manual.In this case, the minister highlighted a series of human errors that proved catastrophic.Crucially, at one point a controller instructed a stalled train to restart, clearing it to advance at up to 160km/h (100 mph) even though a second train was stuck on the line up ahead.The impending collision was clear from audio calls and on big screens in the control centre in Madrid."They worked. We checked. They could see what was happening," Puente confirmed. But the advancing train was never ordered to stop."I'm no judge... But these are the facts."So would he take personal and political responsibility anyway, and resign? Puente called it his "duty", rather, to remain as minister."I'll face up to things, explain, elucidate," he countered. "I'll think how to improve the system, and give confidence to those who want to travel by train and feel calm and safe."But Spaniards will take a lot of persuading."This is not only a very serious accident, but the second in a very short time," Paco Camas of the pollster Ipsos points out.An investigation into January's crash in Adamuz, near Cordoba, is still open, with initial reports suggesting there was a crack in the rails -  very different to the latest collision.But there is a similar impact."It destroys people's confidence not only in the railways but institutions in general," Camas warns. "And in Spain when such things happen, we know that people blame their government."For Team Sánchez it is the latest in a spiral of crises.Allegations of corruption against the prime minister's close relatives still persist, all denied.Then there was a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco this summer to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. That got right-wing opponents shouting about incompetence and underfunding.Later, a video of a pensioner being forcibly evicted from her home went viral and sparked street protests.That's when Sánchez called an early election.His chances of winning the vote looked slim even before the train crash. Now they have plummeted.Most recent polls showed the centre-right PP coming first and forming a coalition with the far-right Vox."They have this majority in almost 95% of the simulations we have done," Prof Pablo Simon of Madrid's Carlos III University explains.But Sánchez had been running a positive campaign, trying to lure apathetic voters to the polls to vote socialist.Suddenly, the tone has changed."They've totally lost control of the agenda and the emotion of this campaign," Simon says. "It's going to be extremely difficult now. There is this general mood of decay, of a country that's not working properly. A depression."There is also anger.There have already been small protests over the train crash led by far-right groups in Madrid and large numbers of police are on stand-by this weekend ahead of further potential clashes, organised online.Here in Toledo, the mood is nervous."We all travelled in silence and really sad," Paloma told me at the city station, where she had just pulled in on a half empty train.She admitted she's scared of the high-speed network now and angry at the government."This crash will change all of our votes, completely," Paloma said. "We'll shift from the left wing to the right. Because of everything that's happened."Lucia takes the high-speed AVE into Madrid each day, and is scared too."This was human error. But there's been two accidents now with more than 100 dead," she says. "Things here are really bad. They have to change."Producer Davide Ghiglione contributed to this report

schema.headline: Spain train disaster clouds Pedro Sánchez chances of re-election

title: The Californian whose pumpkin patch dream took root in Fife
description: Image source, Cairnie Fruit FarmImage caption, The American tradition of pumpkin-picking has become an autumnal tradition for many ScotsByJamie Calder
body: Image source, Cairnie Fruit FarmImage caption, The American tradition of pumpkin-picking has become an autumnal tradition for many ScotsByJamie CalderBBC Scotland NewsWhen Cameron Laird introduced pumpkin-picking to her husband John's farm 28 years ago, she was trying to bring a treasured piece of her American childhood to her new Scottish home.She remembered the dozens of pumpkin farms that lined the roads near her home in California and was keen to bring the tradition to Scotland where it had not yet taken root. Almost three decades later, Cairnie Fruit Farm near Cupar in Fife grows 20,000 pumpkins every year and welcome thousands of visitors from all over Scotland and beyond.The success of Cameron's idea reflects a wider boom in pumpkin patches, with many farmers now diversifying into "experiences" that draw crowds long after other crops are harvested.Image source, Cairnie Fruit FarmImage caption, Farmers like Cameron are experimenting with different sizes, colours and types of pumpkinJohn Laird's family farm had offered pick-your-own experiences for decades before he met Cameron but it had always concentrated on signature Scottish produce such as strawberries and brambles.It was his new wife who suggested the move into pumpkins as an experimental way to boost the farm's income - and as a bit of fun inspired by her US childhood. "I have such fond memories," Cameron told the BBC."I grew up in California and over the hills from us to a place called Half Moon Bay, there must have been 10 or 15 pumpkin farms," she said."You would drive along and just choose one and then there were pumpkins as far as your eye could see. "It was a very vivid part of my childhood and I thought, 'oh, we should do this. We're on a farm, and let's give it a go'."Image source, Cairnie Fruit FarmImage caption, Cairnie Fruit Farm now grows close to 20,000 pumpkins each year, up from just 232 in its first yearCameron and John met when the kilt-wearing Scottish farmer was in California for a friend's wedding.They married and Cameron relocated to Fife where she initially looked for jobs in the Scottish media industry.She had no farming background but was eventually persuaded to join family business – something she said had turned out to be a "very good decision". Image source, Cairnie Fruit FarmImage caption, Cameron (left) came up with the pumpkin patch idea for her family's farm more than 27 years agoDespite Scotland's climate being significantly windier, wetter and colder than her native west coast of the US, her Fife pumpkin patch has grown from just over 200 in its first year to almost 20,000 now. There are also plans in place to extend it out a further acre – making space for about 5,000 more pumpkins.This year they are predicting more than 18,500 visitors to the pumpkin-picking, giving the farm an additional revenue stream through the autumn months and pushing annual pick-your-own visits above 105,000.Image source, Gairneybank FarmImage caption, Farmers across Scotland are turning to pumpkin patches to boost their incomesCameron says pumpkin-picking has also grown into a major social media success, with young Scots flocking to the Cupar field "all decked out in white hats and leather boots" to take photos.She says Fife's cold and often windy weather hasn't put off the crowds. "Scots are intrepid," Cameron says.For many people the chilly weather and needing to get dressed up in thick, cosy clothes is part of the appeal, she says."Not to sound cheesy, but it's all about creating those memories and taking photos," Cameron says.Another farmer who is part of the pumpkin boom is Mike King, the owner of a small cattle and grains farm near Kinross.His patch started as a hobby but has turned out to be a shrewd financial decision."I was getting a bit bored to be honest doing what I was doing," he says."It seemed like the same humdrum, year in, year out."Image source, Gairneybank FarmImage caption, Mike King started the patch at Gairneybank Farm after getting a 'notion for pumpkins'Mike says he got a "notion for pumpkins" about two years ago, deciding to take a chance and experiment with a handful of seeds he bought from Amazon.The next year he grew more than 4,000 and he's now up to 5,000 this autumn. "They're great things to watch growing," he says. "I really enjoy it."This year he's expanded out from the classic orange pumpkins to now have about 12 varieties on his patch at Gairneybank."I've got yellow ones, I've got knobbly ones, bobbly ones, whites, pinks," he says.He also has a range of sizes, saying this year's warmer summer has led to some of his biggest crops, even finding one weighing in at 33kg - around the same as an average 10-year-old child. Image source, Gairneybank FarmImage caption, Some of Mike King's knobbly and bobbly pumpkins from his patch at Gairneybank Farm, near KinrossMike says that expanding his patch could see his income rise but that is not his top priority. "Everyone seems quite happy," he says. "It's more of a relaxed thing than a wild day out, but it seems to be working at the moment."The farming in itself is quite a lonely existence. I'm here myself every day on my own, so this is totally different to me. "You're meeting all these nice people and it's very social. It is work, yes, but it doesn't feel like work. "You are having a chat with people and spending time with them, it's good, I really enjoy it."

schema.headline: The Californian whose pumpkin patch dream took root in Fife

title: Mexico City Grand Prix practice result: Max Verstappen says Liam Lawson collision 'not very smart'
description: Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were both given one-place grid penalties for an incident in which they collided in Friday practice at the Mexico City G
body: Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were both given one-place grid penalties for an incident in which they collided in Friday practice at the Mexico City Grand Prix.Verstappen accused Lawson of "not very smart behaviour" and trying to "drive me off the track at the hairpin" as the two disputed the same piece of track during the session.The four-time champion and the New Zealander clashed in the stadium section towards the end of the lap, with the two cars hitting each other side-on after running through three corners side by side.Race stewards decided that both had been at fault for the incident and took the unusual step of issuing a sporting penalty for an infringement in practice.The FIA stewards report said that Verstappen was preparing for a flying lap and Lawson on a "cool-down" lap after a timed lap "preparing for another push lap".It added: "The drivers of both cars behaved in a manner that was considered unacceptable by the stewards."It said: "Both drivers admitted the moves were unnecessary and 'clumsy'."Verstappen, speaking before the stewards' verdict, said: "Maybe not very smart behaviour what he was trying to do there."At the end of the day it is not going to change my weekend, but if I were him I would act a little smarter and when you're fighting for your seat it's not very smart behaviour."Lawson is one of three drivers competing for two seats at Racing Bulls, Red Bull's junior team, next year, alongside current team-mate Arvid Lindblad and Bulgarian Formula 2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov, who drove for Racing Bulls in first practice on Friday.Verstappen has an influential position within the Red Bull organisation as their star driver.The Dutchman added: "When he saw me coming, he suddenly started to accelerate. I don't know what was going through his head, that he wanted to drive me off the track in the hairpin."That's not very sensible behaviour from someone in his position, to pick a fight with me."Lawson was Verstappen's team-mate for two races at the start of 2025 before being dropped back down to the Racing Bulls junior team after disappointing performances.He had a second spell alongside Verstappen for three races this year as a substitute for regular driver Isack Hadjar after the Frenchman broke his wrist. Lawson acquitted himself more effectively on his second time in the senior team.Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane said: "One word - unnecessary. And I say that of both of them. I haven't heard what Max has said. I'm sure he's got his opinions and I'm sure Liam has his opinion. But mine is, it's just not needed and they can both do better."Ferrari's Charles Leclerc headed McLaren's Lando Norris in the times. Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli, who is poised to clinch his first world title on Sunday, was fourth fastest behind team-mate George Russell.Antonelli's expected coronation is the main event of the weekend - only a victory by Russell or Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton can theoretically stop Antonelli becoming champion on Sunday. Even then, Antonelli only needs ninth place if Russell wins and 10th if Hamilton does.Leclerc, who topped both sessions on Friday, was 0.103 seconds quicker than Norris, with Russell just 0.003secs further adrift.Antonelli was 0.217secs off the pace, and ahead of the Red Bulls of Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.Leclerc's team-mate Lewis Hamilton was 11th overall after stopping on track with a technical problem before completing his qualifying simulation runs on the soft tyre."I was feeling really good in the car," said Hamilton. "It's just my luck."We did a really good job of getting the set-up in a better place. It's just really unfortunate. I think we're really competitive this weekend as a team and then didn't get to do the long run so I have no idea. It's really difficult to overtake here."Russell said: "Ferrari are looking strongest at the moment, Leclerc didn't properly finish his lap. Lewis has the issue. We expected on this sort of circuit for them to perform best but Q3 as it stands can go any way."Behind Hadjar, Racing Bulls duo Arvid Lindblad and Lawson sandwiched Pierre Gasly's Alpine, while McLaren's Oscar Piastri completed the top 10.On the race-simulation runs later in the session, Leclerc again appeared to be the fastest, but the top four teams were all very closely matched and there looked to be little to choose between the soft and medium tyres.The runs suggested a one-stop is the most likely strategy on Sunday and overtaking will be difficult because of the challenge of staying close to another car when overheating is such a challenge in the thin air at the 2,200m altitude of Mexico City.The first session was marked by 10 of the 11 teams running 'rookie' drivers in their cars.One of them was Cadillac's Colton Herta, who the team are considering promoting to a race seat in place of Valtteri Bottas next season.Initially, the team felt his running in Mexico had given him enough points under the F1 system to earn a 'superlicence', which is required to race in F1.But further investigation by governing body the FIA revealed the American nine-time Indycar race winner is still one point short and will have to complete one further practice session this year to secure his licence.The team plan to do that before the end of the season at one of the forthcoming races.

schema.headline: Mexico City Grand Prix practice result: Max Verstappen says Liam Lawson collision 'not very smart'

title: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on
description: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on
body: Dan C, a physiotherapist in Maryland, started his emergency supply after becoming a father. So far, he has spent about $6,000 (£4,470), storing it on shelves in his basement."It's part of my responsibility as a parent," says Dan, 38, who has two children under 10.A few years ago his house was cut off during a "very cold" February and the family was without power for two days. Though he'd already started keeping supplies, "there were numerous gaps in what I had prepared for," he says.Dan's stash now includes 150 gallons of water and several large water storage containers made of soft plastic, which can be filled and kept in the bath. He also keeps things like chlorine dioxide tablets, which are often used to make water from streams or rivers safe to drink.His "rotating pantry" - consisting of long-life food supplies like oats, quinoa and peanut butter - is regularly used for cooking then replaced so "it's not just sitting there expiring". For his family-of-four, he has about three months of food supplies.Dan also has solar panels, a camping stove, a tent, wood supplies and a propane fireplace insert that can run off grid - without electricity or wood. He also keeps extensive medical supplies - including bleeding control kits.In the US, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, external advises people to assemble an emergency kit, make a family emergency plan, and be informed about how to respond to different incidents.Dan says when it comes to emergency planning, "there can be a tendency to catastrophise," but for him, it's about being a "responsible homeowner".Ayumi T, who lives in Tokyo, has kept an emergency bag for years in case of events like earthquakes, typhoons and extreme heat. But after an earthquake in 2024 killed hundreds of people and caused widespread damage to Japan's Noto Peninsula, Ayumi stocked up even more.Tokyo's government has a 68-page disaster prevention guide, external, which details what to keep in an emergency kit and what to do in certain emergency situations.In her emergency rucksack - kept in her wardrobe - Ayumi keeps clothes, towels, menstrual products, disposable chopsticks, sticky notes, disposable masks and a disposable toilet, like those used by hikers and campers."A lot of it is old stuff I don't use anymore," Ayumi, 27, who works at a university, says.Every new year, her family check their kits and update them if necessary, replacing out-of-date food, for example.Over the past five years, "it's been on my mind, 'what happens in case of emergency?'", Nicole Bonds says.The leadership coach in Atlanta, puts this down to noticing "significantly more and more" severe weather patterns and storms around the world and a lack of preparedness.Her motto is "don't panic, be prepared", she says.As well as a large selection of cleaning and hygiene products, Nicole, 48, has bought batteries, a power bank, first-aid supplies, rechargeable fans, blankets and sleeping bags.To keep it affordable she picks up a small amount of supplies "here and there" to gradually build up her stock. She keeps some of the items under her bed, in packing bags and in her kitchen cabinets.Where Michael Stuut lives in the Netherlands is below sea level. He says he worries about extreme weather but also possible war.The 39-year-old, who lives in Hoorn with his wife and five-year-old son, started preparing his kit a few years ago.Michael keeps a healthy stash of power equipment as well as food - including a Starlink Mini, a small and lightweight satellite device for internet access.He keeps supplies in his attic and a crawl space under the house - here lies about 120 litres of water, cash, a first-aid kit and a generator.Earlier this year, Michael created an app to log his food supplies and when they might expire."Being prepared isn't about panic," he says. "It's about being the calm one when the lights go out."In late 2025, Dutch authorities launched a campaign that instructed households to have 72 hours' worth of supplies, much like UK authorities have just done.At the beginning of his prepping journey, Michael's wife didn't see the need, but he says she now understands the importance. They've told their five-year-old the supplies are simply for when they don't want to go to the shop, adding they "don't want to burden him".Michael is sceptical of the three-day advice - also recommended by the UK - but says: "Every household that has a few basic things at home makes it easier for the emergency services to help the people who need it most."Additional reporting by Hanae Takahashi and Richard Frost

schema.headline: How to prepare for an emergency: What households in different countries stock up on

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Rush to recover stolen $6bn' and 'War on wind farms'
description: The Daily Mail leads on further allegations, external against the Duchess of Sussex's father, Thomas Markle. Under the headline "Vault of Shame" the p
body: The Daily Mail leads on further allegations, external against the Duchess of Sussex's father, Thomas Markle. Under the headline "Vault of Shame" the paper says it has reported Markle to the FBI after its journalists uncovered what it called a "stash" of child pornography in a storage unit the paper says was rented by him in Mexico.The Sun says it has been told by staff at the care home, external where Thomas Markle has been living that he has been asked to leave, and is now staying at a different home, in Florida. Markle has strongly denied allegations that he has possessed images of child abuse.In his Guardian article, Andy Burnham offers, external what the paper says amounts to a personal apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade. The prime minister says he will launch an initiative to help the Commonwealth's poorest countries repay their debts, over a longer period of time, with better rates. Ruling out financial reparations, Burnham says he does not think "British people today can be held liable for historical wrongs, however heinous".Leading the Times, Chancellor John Healey vows, external to veto new clean energy projects, if there is a risk the grid cannot cope with the electricity generated pushing up costs for consumers. The chancellor says there is "no sense in building power that can't connect and then paying to switch it off". The paper's editorial notes that wind farms were allowed to connect to the network before upgrades to the national grid had been carried out.The Daily Telegraph says several Red Wall Labour MPs, external are calling on the government to reduce the benefits bill, and not to appease what one calls the "leafy Surrey suburbs". Another MP tells the paper the government should be "ambitious", adding that the UK needed a "Beveridge report for the 21st century".The Daily Mirror leads on a report that the King's niece, external, Zara Tindall, has a jewellery range that features gems from an Australian mine that has been criticised over pollution. "Zara and the Toxic Diamonds" is the headline. The paper says Zara Tindall's agent did not respond to a request for comment.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Rush to recover stolen $6bn' and 'War on wind farms'

title: Jamie Carragher sued: Aston Villa to take legal action against pundit over 'unacceptable insults'
description: Aston Villa say they will initiate legal action against former England defender Jamie Carragher over what they describe as "unacceptable insults".Vill
body: Aston Villa say they will initiate legal action against former England defender Jamie Carragher over what they describe as "unacceptable insults".Villa made the announcement in a statement on social media - signed by chairman Nassef Sawiris - in which they accused Carragher of insulting the club and their fans.The club said they would "not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football".Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast earlier this week, Carragher suggested Villa boss Unai Emery would be interested in becoming Manchester United head coach.United boss Michael Carrick's position is hanging in the balance after a dismal start to the season.Referring to former Paris St-Germain and Arsenal boss Emery, Carragher said: "Surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again."There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not."So Real Madrid will take Manchester United's best player, they did it with [Cristiano] Ronaldo. And there will be teams below Aston Villa, and they'll take their players or manager, so shut the [expletive] up Aston Villa fans. Aston Villa will never be Manchester United."Former Liverpool defender Carragher, who works as a pundit for Sky Sports and American broadcaster CBS, was criticised by Villa fans for his comments.Responding to that criticism on social media, he said telling them to shut up had been "a joke" after "the stick Villa fans have given me over saying Emery may fancy joining Man Utd".Carragher, 48, added he had been praising Emergy and Villa "for years".He expanded on that on the Overlap Daily, saying: "I just think Unai Emery is the best manager in the league and if you're Man Utd you're thinking 'what's the best we can get?'. "I'm not saying he'll go - I'm just saying if it was me I'd ask the question."I think your own ego if someone said 'that's your level' would say 'no I'm not'. That was my point. It's grown arms and legs."Carragher reiterated his message to Villa fans had been meant "in jest".

schema.headline: Jamie Carragher sued: Aston Villa to take legal action against pundit over 'unacceptable insults'

title: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentRepo
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, Arnon Nampa dressed as Harry Potter at the protest in August 2020 ByJonathan HeadSouth East Asia correspondentReporting fromBangkokEven before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending."To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A drawing by Arnon Nampa's 10-year-old daughter showing her father in prisonThe past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions."If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Arnon at a protest in 2023From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son."Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom." Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's family, drawn by his daughter, titled "heading to court". Her mum is carrying a poster that says, "Free my dad"The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.That changed on 3 August 2020.That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, Arnon's reunion with his family, as drawn by his daughterOne of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame. She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy."I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve."I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté."It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."Image source, GoodmondayshootImage caption, Melinn doing the three-finger salute in August 2020Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.She joined a movement calling itself Thalu Wang, which translates as "breaking through the palace". Instead of giving speeches, they came up with stunts like holding polls on the street, asking people what they thought of royal motorcades holding up the traffic, or whether they believed the monarchy had too much power."We knew the risks, but we thought it would be safer just conducting a poll. It turns out it was not."She was given two more lèse majesté charges in 2022, and detained before being released on bail. She had to wear an electronic monitor on her ankle and was barred from leaving her home between 4pm and 6am. Her parents were forced to sign a document promising to inform on her. She was facing decades in jail. Melinn decided she had no choice. With a friend she fled Thailand and eventually got asylum in Canada.Image source, Arnon Nampa's familyImage caption, A painting by Arnon's daughter titled "my dad's feelings"Article 112 is on paper just a law, like any other, passed by the Thai parliament, which can, theoretically, be amended by elected MPs. In fact it has been amended in the past, notably in 1976 when the punishment for breaking it was increased to between three and 15 years in prison.But today the Constitutional Court has decreed that the law itself, like the institution it protects, is untouchable. The reformist Move Forward party - the successor of Future Forward - was dissolved in 2024, and its leader banned from politics, merely for proposing that the punishments be less harsh. And the courts make it very difficult for those charged under it to defend themselves."In many cases, like the one against Arnon Nampa, prosecutors accuse the defendant of lying about the monarchy," says Chaimaneekarakate, the lawyer. "But when we ask the judge to subpoena documents or witnesses who could show the truth of what the defendant says, the judge refuses to do it. When one lawyer protested against the court deciding that the trial would be held in secret, she was warned by the judge to be quiet or face a contempt of court charge."He says judges sometimes criticise the young activists over their alleged actions even before the trial has started.Image source, Arnon NampaImage caption, Arnon has been writing letters to his children since he was jailed three years agoAs the one who ignited the debate about the monarchy Arnon appears to be getting the harshest punishment. Despite the formidable odds stacked against him he still prepares carefully for every court appearance, taking part in his own defence and helping other inmates with theirs. This isn't easy; he is not allowed to bring any of his written notes, and must memorise all his arguments.The judges object to him playing the part of a lawyer in his regulation-brown prison shorts, his feet bare and shackled. But it does give him an opportunity to see his family.The letters he writes are the only other way he stays in touch with them. He may spend his entire life in prison. He wants his children to know him, and to understand, when they are older, why he chose to challenge the system and lose his freedom."Since the first day that we made up our mind to take up this mission, we knew of the dangers. Speaking the truth is not difficult. What is difficult is speaking a forbidden truth. I remember well that on the evening of 3 August 2020, after speaking at the Harry Potter event, I felt very good, content, and relieved to have finally begun speaking about the truth, in public," he wrote to his family last year.Earlier this year, he wrote: "Living here is a struggle. But it is just a dot in the bigger picture of our movement's struggle. We must play a part in writing our own history. Become a drop of water that will one day become an ocean."

schema.headline: Lèse majesté: Arnon Nampa questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years

title: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
description: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, Seven celebrities remained at the start of the final episodeByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpd
body: Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, Seven celebrities remained at the start of the final episodeByIan YoungsCulture reporterUpdated 7 hours agoSpoiler warning: This story reveals details of The Celebrity Traitors finalWe've had four weeks of suspense, suspicion and very suspect tactics, as some of Britain's biggest stars engaged in a battle of wits to win the most popular show on TV.The second series of BBC One's The Celebrity Traitors reached its climax on Friday, with the 21 original contestants having been reduced to seven before the final.They were then whittled down to two winners - with the faithful duo of comedian Romesh Ranganathan and Heartstopper actor Sebastian "Bash" Croft emerging victorious.The players successfully banished the remaining traitors - Love Island host Maya Jama and YouTuber King Kenny - in dramatic fashion, and the winning pair shared the £83,000 prize for their charities.Image source, Paul Chappells/ Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, Romesh Ranganathan and Sebastian "Bash" Croft celebrated with host Claudia WinklemanFigure caption, What just happened in Celebrity Traitors final?As it happened: Relive the Celebrity Traitors finalWatch The Celebrity Traitors on BBC iPlayerGet all the reaction on Uncloaked on BBC iPlayerMore than 15 million people have been tuning in to this series.Kenny reached the final stage, the endgame, after turning on his fellow traitor Maya at the last round table.Kenny, Romesh and Bash were joined by singer James Blunt in the climax of the endgame, where the remaining contestants gather around a fire pit to decide whether they think there are any traitors left.When James and Kenny were tied in a vote for who was a traitor, Bash persuaded Romesh to banish Kenny instead of James - thereby securing victory for team faithful."Absolutely devastated. Almost scraped it," Kenny seethed. "I was so close, I smelled the victory." However, he can take consolation from the fact his performance on the show has established him as a mainstream star.Figure caption, The final reveal of the Celebrity TraitorsIn a further twist, James chose another round of voting and was subsequently evicted himself, leaving Romesh and Bash as the last men standing."This might actually be the best day of my life," said 24-year-old Bash through tears of joy.He, too, can expect a major career boost.Romesh reflected: "I just really hope my mum's proud. And also my youngest son Charlie, who wanted me to come on the show - dad won. Please show me some respect."The pair will split their winnings between two refugee charities, the Refugee Council and Choose Love.Image source, Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, Traitors Kenny and Maya fell at the final hurdleImage source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Paul ChappellsImage caption, The final six: Maya, James, Kenny, Romesh, Leigh-Anne and BashEarlier, actor Michael Sheen was murdered in the first action of Friday's episode. "I am incredibly disappointed," he said. "Gutted that I got so close to the end. It's been absolutely unforgettable."When it came to the endgame, Little Mix singer Leigh-Anne Pinnock was swiftly banished after Kenny voted to remove her."I was thinking me and him had a mutual understanding, and now I feel so stupid," she raged."But I'm walking away feeling super proud and like I've really accomplished something here."Image source, BBC/Studio Lambert/Euan CherryImage caption, James Blunt helped retrieve the final prize money in a mission involving dynamite and helicoptersMeanwhile, James B was left rueing one final mistake in a long but valiant catalogue of misjudgements throughout the series.The singer, who looked aghast when he was attacked by Romesh during the endgame, was then the only one to choose to banish again when it came to the final three.James was unaware that Romesh and Bash had both chosen to end the game - meaning he too could have been a winner if he had done the same - but became the victim of his own choice to banish."I've loved trying to work it out, I've loved getting it wrong so often, I've loved the tiny moments when I've got it right," he said wistfully. "I've loved the game."Image source, Euan Cherry/Studio Lambert/BBCImage caption, James Acaster effectively banished himself in a novel twist in the showCelebrities who departed earlier in the series included ex-EastEnders actor Ross Kemp, model Jerry Hall, sitcom star Miranda Hart, comedian Joe Lycett, presenter Hannah Fry and former BBC journalist Amol Rajan.This series is also likely to be remembered for the two contestants who made the unorthodox decision to reveal themselves as traitors, before being summarily dispatched by their fellow players.First, actor Richard E Grant was so giddy to have received the tap on the shoulder that he blurted out his supposedly secret status in episode two.Comedian James Acaster, meanwhile, was the most reluctant traitor in the history of The Traitors, and unexpectedly gave himself up when he came under pressure at the round table in Thursday's penultimate episode.Aftermath of Acaster's admission There have been reports, external that filming of the scene was paused and he was checked by welfare staff after he became anxious.Asked about the reports, a BBC spokesperson said on Friday that the safety and welfare of those taking part was the "highest priority", and "players are closely monitored and supported throughout by production which includes a dedicated and experienced welfare team".Speculation about the round table being heavily edited was fuelled when eagle-eyed viewers noticed, external a shot of Romesh reacting in shock - apparently to James A's initial confession - which in fact seemed to have come from a later moment, after Romesh had voted for James by writing his name on the blackboard.In the episode, the sequence where the celebrities all voted for James in light of his admission was shown as a relatively quick and straightforward process, raising a question about what prompted Romesh's shocked look.Acaster did not take part in Friday's edition of spin-off show Uncloaked, which reunited some of the celebrity contestants following the final.'A bit dull?'The comedian's bombshell the previous night did provide the programme with a twist to spark it to life after what some viewers saw as a mid-series lull.On Thursday, the Hollywood Reporter noted, external that the show had achieved record-breaking ratings - before asking: "Why, then, has much of the consensus on social media been that it's all felt a bit dull?"Some noted a shortage of true back-stabbing, double-crossing and explosive rows - the things, in other words, that viewers love the most - while the celebrities were more chummy and savvy than previous groups of castle dwellers.And while there was no shortage of big characters, this season lacked an equivalent to Alan Carr, the hugely popular and apparently hapless comedian who lied and murdered his way to an unlikely victory as a traitor last year.The drama ramped up in the final, though, and Friday's episode is likely to have been the most watched TV programme of the year.

schema.headline: Celebrity Traitors comes to a climax in nail-biting final
